items.question: How are these practitioners classified and how do they attain the state of Shiva?
premises: The practitioners are to be known as twofold: worldly and initiated.
The former, the worldly ones, would gradually become Shivas.
The others, the initiated ones, become Shivas from that experience alone.
items.inference: Both worldly and initiated practitioners can attain the state of Shiva, but the initiated do so immediately through experience while the worldly do so gradually.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'that experience' (tadbhoga) is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: They are to be known as twofold: worldly and initiated. The former would gradually become Shivas, while the others become Shivas from that experience alone.

items.question: How does initiation produce different results for yogins?
premises: Initiiation is divided by higher, lower, and many other distinctions.
This division operates through the power of its application.
Such divided initiation gives varied fruits to yogins.
items.inference: The diversity of initiatory forms leads to a corresponding diversity of spiritual results for practitioners.
items.plain_english: Initiation, being divided by higher, lower, and many other distinctions, would give varied fruits to yogins according to the power of those divisions.

items.question: How are the knowers divided and what happens to those with trembling knowledge at death?
premises: The knowers here are divided twofold into trembling and other.
Among them are those whose knowledge is of the trembling kind.
Those trembling knowers clearly become Shivas at the end of the body.
items.inference: Even knowers whose realization is still unstable attain the state of Shiva at the time of death.
uncertainties: The exact nature of 'trembling knowledge' (kampravijñāna) is explained in the following verses.
items.plain_english: But the knowers here are twofold, divided into trembling and other. Among them, those whose knowledge is trembling clearly become Shivas at the end of the body.

rows.morph: vijñānam n.nom.sg + eteṣām m.gen.pl + utpannam n.nom.sg

items.question: Why is the knowledge of the trembling knowers described as unstable?
premises: Knowledge has arisen in these practitioners.
Their knowledge is not very clear because it is connected with other thoughts.
Their knowledge is also not uprooted in its nature.
items.inference: The trembling knowers have genuine but incomplete realization, still mixed with conceptual thought and not fully eradicated of latent tendencies.
items.plain_english: Because knowledge has arisen in them, but it is not very clear due to connection with other thoughts, nor is its nature completely uprooted.

items.question: What happens to residual conceptual thought at death for the trembling knower?
premises: Conceptual thought arises in the body from carelessness.
At the fall of the body, that conceptual thought necessarily perishes.
When it perishes, supreme knowledge is recognized.
items.inference: Death removes the bodily basis of residual conceptual disturbance, allowing the already-arisen supreme knowledge to stand revealed.
items.plain_english: Therefore, conceptual thought that arises in the body from carelessness would necessarily perish at the fall of the body, and then supreme knowledge is recognized.

items.question: How does mature knowledge manifest when its obstruction is removed?
premises: Knowledge may remain within, not destroyed, while standing among latent impressions and thoughts.
Such knowledge can reach ripeness.
When the obstruction is removed, that ripe knowledge shines forth.
items.inference: Liberating knowledge can be present in a mature but obstructed form and becomes fully manifest once the obstruction disappears.
items.plain_english: That knowledge, standing within undestroyed among latent impressions and thoughts and having reached ripeness, indeed shines forth when the obstruction is removed.

items.question: Why do those established in well-practiced knowledge have no concern at death?
premises: Some practitioners are made of well-practiced knowledge and are always of the nature of Shiva.
They are indeed liberated while living.
For them there is no deliberation at all at the time of death.
items.inference: Because the jivanmuktas are already established in Shiva-nature, death introduces no new spiritual issue requiring deliberation.
items.plain_english: But those who are made of well-practiced knowledge and are always of the nature of Shiva are indeed liberated while living; for them there is no deliberation at all at death.

items.question: How is the absence of deliberation at death compared to the jivanmukta's state in life?
premises: For the liberated while living, there is no deliberation in life regarding happiness, unhappiness, or delusion.
Death is presented as analogous to that living state.
Therefore there is no such deliberation at death either.
items.inference: The jivanmukta's freedom from reactive deliberation is continuous across both life and death.
items.plain_english: Just as there is no deliberation for the liberated while living in states of happiness, unhappiness, or delusion, so too there is no such deliberation at death.

items.question: Which scriptural authorities are cited to support the teaching on the knower's liberation?
premises: The Supreme Lord said this in the holy Ratnamala scripture.
The Lord Ahi, bearer of the burden of supporting the world, also said it in his own scripture.
items.inference: The teaching about the knower's liberation is supported by multiple authoritative scriptural sources.
uncertainties: The identification of 'Ahi-lord' and 'his own scripture' depends on tradition-specific attribution.
items.plain_english: The Supreme Lord said this in the holy Ratnamala scripture, and the Lord Ahi, bearer of the burden of supporting the world, also said it in his own scripture.

items.question: Does the place or mental state at death affect the knower's attainment of liberation?
premises: The knower may die in places considered impure or inauspicious, such as a street, filth, an outcaste's house, hell, or a cremation ground.
At that time the knower may be with thought or without thought.
Even so, the knower obtains liberation at the end.
items.inference: For the knower, liberation is not dependent on external purity of place or on the presence or absence of discursive thought at death.
items.plain_english: Whether in a street, amid urine and feces, in an outcaste's house, in hell, or in a cremation ground, and whether with thought or without thought, the knower obtains liberation even at the end.

rows.morph: dhvaniḥ m.nom.sg + jīvanmuktatām f.acc.sg + asya m.gen.sg

items.question: What does the phrase 'even' in the cited passage indicate about the knower's state?
premises: The particle 'even' in the citation carries an expressive force.
That force indicates the knower's state of living liberation.
The mention of being with thought or without thought indicates a possible condition, not a limitation.
items.inference: The scriptural citation affirms that the knower's liberation is already established, so varying mental states at death do not alter it.
items.plain_english: The word 'even' expresses his state of living liberation, and the mention of being with thought or without thought indicates only a possible condition.

items.question: What is the final state of one liberated simultaneously with knowledge, regardless of place or memory at death?
premises: One may abandon the body at a holy place or in the house of a dog-cooker.
One may even have lost memory at the time of death.
One who is liberated simultaneously with knowledge goes to absolute isolation, free from sorrow.
items.inference: For one liberated in the very moment of knowledge, neither place nor memory at death affects the attainment of sorrowless absolute isolation.
items.plain_english: Whether at a holy place or in the house of a dog-cooker, even if memory is lost, one who abandons the body and is liberated simultaneously with knowledge goes to absolute isolation, with sorrow destroyed.
